t: Number of Sub-arrays of Size K and Average >= Threshold — Sliding Window Editorial
o: We must count fixed-size windows of length $k$ whose average is at least `threshold`. Since the window size is fixed, comparing the average to the threshold is equivalent to comparing the window **sum** to $k \cdot threshold$, which avoids floating-point division entirely. In Example 1 ($k=3$, threshold=4), the target sum is 12; windows [2,5,5], [5,5,5], [5,5,8] have sums 12, 15, 18 and qualify. In Example 2 the target sum is 15 and the first six windows all exceed it. With $n$ up to $10^5$, an $O(nk)$ brute force may be too slow in the worst case, motivating a sliding-window / prefix-sum approach that runs in $O(n)$.
k: Comparing average to threshold is equivalent to comparing window sum to k * threshold — use integers only, no precision issues.
Fixed-size sub-arrays are a textbook sliding window: add the entering element, remove the leaving element each step.
Prefix sums let you get any window sum in O(1): sum(i..i+k-1) = prefix[i+k] - prefix[i].

a.i: Build a prefix-sum array so any window sum can be computed in constant time as the difference of two prefixes. Then slide over every valid start index and count windows whose sum meets $k \cdot threshold$. This is simple and robust, at the cost of $O(n)$ extra memory.
s: Compute target = k * threshold (use a wide type to avoid overflow).
Build prefix where prefix[i] = arr[0] + ... + arr[i-1], with prefix[0] = 0.
For each i from 0 to n - k, compute windowSum = prefix[i+k] - prefix[i].
Increment the answer whenever windowSum >= target.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to build prefix sums plus one pass over all window starts.
a.sp: O(n) — extra array of size n+1 for prefix sums.

a.i: Instead of storing all prefix sums, maintain just the current window's sum. Slide the window one position at a time: add the incoming element and subtract the outgoing one. This keeps the same counting logic but uses constant extra space.
s: Sum the first k elements into windowSum and initialize answer to 1 if windowSum >= k * threshold else 0.
For each right index from k to n-1:
Add arr[right] and subtract arr[right - k] from windowSum.
If windowSum >= k * threshold, increment the answer.
a.t: O(n) — each element enters and leaves the window exactly once.
a.sp: O(1) — only the running window sum and counter are stored.

w: In an interview, mention the brute-force O(nk) idea briefly, then present the sliding window as the optimal solution — it demonstrates you recognize fixed-size window patterns. Key pitfalls: (1) dividing by k and comparing floats instead of using integer comparison against k*threshold; (2) overflow of the window sum in C++/Java when using 32-bit ints (max sum is 10^5 * 10^4 = 10^9, near INT_MAX, so use 64-bit); (3) off-by-one errors on the loop bounds — there are exactly n - k + 1 windows. Edge cases: k equals the array length (answer is 0 or 1), and threshold 0 (every window qualifies since elements are non-negative). Likely follow-ups: generalize to variable-size windows (minimum size sub-array sum), or handle negative numbers (sliding window still works here because the window size is fixed).
